description: Explains stem-cell self-renewal, potency and tissue niches through transplantation and lineage-tracing experiments, intestinal organoids and regenerating animals. Connects nuclear transfer and induced pluripotency to cellular memory while distinguishing tissue-restricted regeneration from whole-organ reconstruction.

historical_claims.anchor: In 2007, Nick Barker, Hans Clevers and their colleagues identified cells expressing a gene called Lgr5 at the base of intestinal crypts in mice.
The marked lineages generated the different epithelial cell types lining the gut over extended observation.
Two years later, Toshiro Sato and colleagues showed that, under the right culture conditions, single Lgr5-positive intestinal cells could generate miniature self-organizing epithelial structures.
In 2011, Daniel Wagner, Irving Wang and Peter Reddien tested the problem with a demanding experiment.

historical_claims.anchor: In 2009, Martin Kragl, Elly Tanaka and colleagues examined the origins of regenerating limb tissues with genetic labeling.
In 1962, John Gurdon transferred nuclei from differentiated frog intestinal cells into egg cells whose own nuclei had been removed or inactivated.
